title: Under the Neem Tree

sections.heading: Beginning
sections.content:
The Zilla Parishad school stood at the edge of the village like a bright blue-and-white box. A large neem tree grew in the courtyard, spreading its branches wide like open arms. Every morning, children gathered under it for assembly, and at lunchtime, they sat in neat rows with steel plates for the midday meal.

Sanika Jadhav loved this school. She loved the dusty playground, the smell of chalk, and most of all, she loved drawing. Her pencil box was stuffed with twelve colored pencils, and she could draw anything: birds, flowers, the Sahyadri hills that rose behind the village like sleeping giants.

One Tuesday morning, their teacher Kavita Bai walked into class with a big smile. She clapped her hands twice, and everyone fell silent.

"Listen carefully, children," she said. "Our school has been chosen for the taluka-level 'Best Village Display' competition. Taluka means all the villages in our area. It will happen during Bail Pola week!"

The class buzzed with excitement. Bail Pola was everyone's favorite festival — the day when families decorated their bullocks with colorful beads and painted horns, fed them sweet puran poli, and paraded them through the village with dhol-tasha drums.

"Each class must prepare a project showing something special about our village," Bai continued. "Work in groups. But remember — a good project needs more than pretty pictures. It needs truth."

Sanika's hand shot up. "Bai, can we draw charts? I can make beautiful pictures!"

In the back row, Rohit Kale sat quietly, looking at his hands. He was a thin boy with careful eyes that noticed everything — the direction of the wind, the color of the clouds, the mood of a bullock. But in the classroom, he felt invisible.

During lunch, Aniket Shinde said loudly, "What will Rohit do for the project? He only knows about mud and bullocks!"

Some boys laughed. Rohit heard them. He pressed his lips together and walked away to sit alone by the school wall.

sections.heading: Middle
sections.content:
Sanika's group decided to make their project about the village's farming life. For three days, Sanika painted bright green fields and golden jowar stalks on chart paper. Another girl, Priya, wrote neat paragraphs about the village. But when they pinned everything on the display board, something felt wrong.

"It looks nice," Priya said slowly, "but it looks like a textbook picture. It doesn't feel like our village."

Sanika stared at the board and knew Priya was right. The drawings were colorful but empty — like a beautiful box with nothing inside.

The next morning, Rohit came to school carrying a cloth bag. Inside were a small piece of sugarcane stalk, a handful of dried jowar grains, and two tiny hand-carved wooden bullocks his grandfather had made. He placed them quietly on his desk.

Sanika noticed. She picked up one of the wooden bullocks. "Rohit, this is beautiful! Your grandfather made this?"

Rohit nodded shyly and showed her the sugarcane and jowar grains. "I thought maybe someone could use them. For the project."

Sanika's eyes went wide. "This is exactly what we need! Our project has drawings but no real things. Will you join our group?"

Rohit looked down. "Aniket said farmers' sons don't know about competitions."

"Aniket is wrong. Your knowledge is the most important part."

Rohit hesitated for a long moment. Then he nodded.

From that day, the project transformed. Rohit explained the cycle of farming — how his father plowed the field before the monsoon, sowed soybean seeds in June, and harvested jowar in winter. He described how the soil smelled different before rain, like wet iron and fresh leaves. Sanika listened carefully and painted each season in bright colors.

Rohit placed the real sugarcane and jowar grains on the display board next to Sanika's paintings. He set his grandfather's wooden bullocks in the center, with a small card that read: "Our bullocks help us farm. On Bail Pola, we thank them."

Priya brought her mother's thecha recipe written on a card. The recipe used green chilies, garlic, peanuts, and salt, all ground on a stone. A boy named Vishal brought a photograph of decorated bullocks from last year's Pola.

One afternoon, Aniket stood watching Rohit explain the farming seasons to the group. He listened as Rohit described how his father woke before sunrise and how the red soil changed color with each season. Aniket looked at his own empty hands. He thought about his mother's kitchen, her careful hands shaping modak dumplings. Maybe he had something to share too.

The next day, Aniket walked over. "Can I add something? My mother makes the best ukdiche modak in the village. I can bring the recipe."

"Yes!" Sanika said. "Everyone should add something."

Bai watched all of this from her desk, smiling.

sections.heading: End
sections.content:
The day of the competition arrived on a bright, clear morning. Judges from the education office came and walked through the school, visiting each classroom's display.

When they reached Sanika and Rohit's class, they stopped. The display board was alive with color and truth. Sanika's paintings showed four seasons of farming. Real jowar grains were glued in neat rows. A piece of sugarcane stood in a small clay pot. The wooden bullocks sat proudly in the center. Around them were recipe cards, photographs, and a hand-drawn map of the village.

"Who will explain this?" asked one of the judges.

Rohit stepped forward. His heart was beating fast, but when he looked at the display — at his grandfather's bullocks, at the jowar his family had grown — he felt a warmth rise in his chest. This was his world. He knew it well.

"This is our village," he began, his voice steady. "We grow sugarcane, soybean, and jowar. The soil here is red, and before the monsoon comes, it smells like iron. On Bail Pola, we decorate our bullocks because they work hard all year. We paint their horns, put bead necklaces on them, and feed them puran poli — sweet flatbread stuffed with jaggery and lentils. It is our way of saying thank you."

Sanika stood beside him, pointing to her illustrations as he spoke. When Rohit finished, the judges clapped.

That afternoon, the results were announced. Their class won second prize — a set of twenty books for the school library. The children cheered so loudly that birds flew out of the neem tree.

After the competition, Aniket walked up to Rohit. "You knew more than all of us. I'm sorry I said those things."

Rohit smiled. "It's okay. You helped too, with the modak recipe."

Three days later, Bail Pola arrived. Rohit's family decorated their bullocks, Shiva and Ganya, painting their horns bright red and yellow and hanging necklaces of colorful beads around their necks. Sanika came running down the red soil path to see them.

"They look magnificent!" she cried.

The whole village paraded their bullocks through the streets. The dhol-tasha players beat their drums, and the sound echoed off the Sahyadri hills. Rohit walked proudly beside Shiva and Ganya, and Sanika walked with him.

At school the next day, Bai stood before the class. "Sanika's drawings were beautiful, but without Rohit's knowledge, they were just pictures. Rohit's knowledge was deep, but without Sanika's art, it had no voice. And without all of you adding your pieces, the project would not have won."

She paused and smiled.

"No knowledge is small. The child who knows the earth knows the world."

Rohit sat at his desk, and for the first time all year, he did not feel invisible. He felt seen.

characters.name: Sanika Jadhav
characters.role: A creative, kind 9-year-old girl who loves drawing and brings the project to life with her art. She recognizes Rohit's value and invites him to join her group.

characters.name: Rohit Kale
characters.role: A quiet, observant 10-year-old boy who helps his family farm sugarcane and soybean. His deep knowledge of farming and nature becomes the heart of the school project.

characters.name: Kavita Bai
characters.role: The warm and wise teacher at the Zilla Parishad school who encourages every child to contribute and believes all knowledge has value.

characters.name: Aniket Shinde
characters.role: A competitive classmate who initially teases Rohit but gradually sees the value of his knowledge, apologizes, and contributes to the project.

vocabulary_words.simple_definition: Changed completely into something much better or different.
Extremely beautiful and impressive to look at.

vocabulary_words.context_sentence: But in the classroom, he felt invisible.
vocabulary_words.simple_definition: Feeling like nobody can see you or notice you are there.

vocabulary_words.context_sentence: The whole village paraded their bullocks through the streets.
vocabulary_words.simple_definition: Walked together in a group through a public place to celebrate or show something.

moral_lesson: Working together and respecting every person's contribution — no matter how small — helps the whole community succeed. True friendship means lifting others up rather than competing against them. No knowledge is small; every person's life experience is valuable.
revisions_made: Added an inline gloss for 'taluka' ('Taluka means all the villages in our area') and simplified 'Block Education Office' to 'education office' to help ESL readers unfamiliar with Indian administrative terms.

Developed Aniket's internal shift by adding a scene where he watches Rohit explain farming to the group, reflects on his own empty hands, and thinks about what he could contribute — making his later apology feel more earned.

Trimmed approximately 340 words from the middle and end sections by condensing the lagori scene, the tiffin/lunch description, the Bail Pola celebration details, and Rohit's presentation speech, improving pacing for ESL readers.

Split the longer compound sentence about Priya's thecha recipe into two clearer sentences: 'Priya brought her mother's thecha recipe written on a card. The recipe used green chilies, garlic, peanuts, and salt, all ground on a stone.'
